fact: Techweez reports that schools entered pathway, subject-combination and senior-school choices against each learner's record on KEMIS for nearly 1.2 million Grade 9 learners, KEMIS being the required platform for the 2026 Grade 10 selection, in an exercise due to close on 11 September 2026.

Techweez states that KEMIS is built to pull together data from early childhood education through to university, where NEMIS mostly served basic education; no date is given, so the publication date is used.
Techweez states that KEMIS is funded through the World Bank-backed Kenya Primary Education Equity in Learning Programme; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

Techweez states that the Ministry of Education describes KEMIS as a government-led project with other state agencies, development partners and unnamed technology providers, and has not named the contractor or published the agreements; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

The Education Principal Secretary told the Public Accounts Committee in late August 2026 that the latest capitation disbursement used neither NEMIS nor KEMIS but manually verified data, because KEMIS was not yet complete.
KEMIS became the required platform for the 2026 Grade 10 selection exercise covering nearly 1.2 million Grade 9 learners, closing on 11 September 2026.

During the Grade 10 selection in September 2026 schools reported failed logins, slow responses, submissions that did not save and learner records showing the previous Grade 9 cohort on KEMIS, and the Ministry sent field officers to monitor while technical teams stabilised it; the number of schools affected is not given.

The Ministry's KEMIS circular tells schools to enter and correct each learner's record in KEMIS themselves: KNEC index or assessment number, names, demographic details and parent or guardian identification, then save and resubmit it for validation; it names no attendance or results entry, and gives no date, so the publication date is used.

The circular is issued by the Ministry of Education, State Department for Basic Education, and signed by the Head of KEMIS, with the ministry's field officers told to support schools; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

The Ministry's circular states that the KEMIS Learner Validation Engine is now operational, marking each learner Valid or Invalid against examination and assessment databases, with a Unique Learner Identifier generated once parent or guardian details are complete; the circular is undated in its body, so the publication date is used.

Data Landscapers' 54-country review (its author's AI-assisted compilation, scoring Kenya's rural schools 1) states that rural primary schools in Kenya predominantly use paper registers for administrative data, attendance and learning outcomes, lacking electricity, internet, computers and trained staff for routine digital entry; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

fact: Development Gateway and IREX report that NEMIS supports the digital registration of learners, with data collected at schools, primarily by teachers, on Google Sheets and submitted electronically, and that interviewees used it to register learners, transfer them between schools and register them for national examinations; no attendance or results entry is described, and no date is given beyond the research period (December 2022 to February 2024), so the publication date is used.

The white paper states that NEMIS's modules capture learners, institutions, finances and teachers for all basic education institutions, primary and secondary; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

A 2021 Treasury education sector report, as cited by the white paper, found that only 65 per cent of primary schools had captured data in NEMIS, against a 90 per cent implementation rate in secondary education; no counts are given.

The white paper states that the Government of Kenya invested heavily in NEMIS, launched in 2017 with assistance from the Global Partnership for Education, and that a stakeholder called it meant for the Ministry and not for the school; the publication date is used.

The white paper states that the government had recently launched a re-engineering of NEMIS, to be renamed KEMIS with a wider scope and a unique identifier for each child from birth, on the recommendation of the Presidential Working Party's 2023 report; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

The World Bank's regional brief states that the percentage of primary schools submitting EMIS data rose from 60 per cent in 2015 to 90 per cent in 2021, under the Kenya GPE Primary Education Development Project; no counts are given, and the figure is schools submitting data, not schools entering attendance or results.

The World Bank states that the project supported the migration of the paper-based EMIS to the online NEMIS and that, in developing it, learners were registered with unique personal identifiers linked to their birth certificates; no attendance or results entry is described, and no date is given beyond the 2021 schools figure.

The World Bank states that the Ministry of Education uses NEMIS data for student placement, disbursement of capitation grants for primary and secondary schools and medical cover for secondary students; no date is given, so the publication date is used.
The World Bank describes NEMIS as the Ministry of Education's EMIS and its data as used by the ministry; no date is given, so the publication date is used.

The World Bank states that the Kenya GPE Primary Education Development Project (P146797) supported the migration of the paper-based EMIS to the online NEMIS; no domestic budget line is mentioned, and the publication date is used.

The World Bank's status report states that learners are registered individually in NEMIS, the birth certificate number being used to generate each student's UPI, and that registration drives capitation grants; it does not say who keys the registration or when in the year.

The World Bank reports that registration of primary school learners in NEMIS is about 60 per cent and of secondary school learners above 98 per cent, and that NEMIS data is used to disburse capitation to primary, junior and secondary schools.

The World Bank gives no share or count of primary schools entering data: its figure is of learners, about 60 per cent of primary school learners registered in NEMIS, so that some primary schools do not receive their full capitation grants; missing birth certificates in the early grades are given as the cause.

The World Bank states that the Ministry of Education, with other government agencies, is reinforcing the registration of all learners in NEMIS, analyses NEMIS data and is responsible for each NEMIS action in the programme's action plan.

The Ministry of Education's sector plan states that the NEMIS platform is being operationalised to support the digital registration of learners; it does not say who keys the registration or when in the year, and gives no date, so the publication year is used.
The sector plan states that primary and secondary school learners have so far been registered on NEMIS; no date is given, so the publication year is used.

The sector plan gives no share or count of primary schools entering data: it says NEMIS has reached a 70 per cent level of operationalisation, without saying of what, and could serve about 84,000 learning institutions; no date is given, so the publication year is used.

The Ministry of Education's plan states that the sector itself designed, developed and rolled out NEMIS, and names the Principal Secretary for Basic Education as lead for developing KEMIS; no date is given, so the publication year is used.

The National Education Sector Strategic Plan 2023-2027 names KEMIS, to hold individual information from birth to the end of education and to take in NEMIS, and carries costed yearly lines in Kenya shillings for developing the system, enhancing its modules, a policy to institutionalise it and data infrastructure.
